section.title: Purpose
section.para: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) describes a single, shared tree: the vendor's programs, locally installed programs and their libraries are placed together under /usr, and one C library serves every program on the system. That model has served UNIX-like systems for three decades, but it makes three things hard:

listitem.para: Separating what the vendor ships from what the user installs. When both write into /usr/bin and /usr/lib, an upgrade of the base system and an install of third-party software can replace each other's files.
Upgrading the base as one unit. A base that is spread across the shared tree is upgraded file by file, while it is running.

Having more than one C library. The paths /lib, /lib64, /usr/include and the dynamic loader location assume a single C library. Installing a second one into the same directories mixes headers, loaders and runtime libraries of two incompatible ABIs.

section.para: The Dualayer Hierarchy Standard (DHS) solves these by giving each part of the system its own layer — a directory tree with a single owner — and by giving each C library its own directory, named after its target triplet. The running system sees the layers as one tree, composed at boot with OverlayFS.

section.title: The name
section.para: Dualayer joins dual and layer: the system is built from layers, and two C libraries — musl and glibc — live in it side by side. The standard is abbreviated DHS.

section.title: Scope

listitem.para: the entries allowed at the root of the filesystem;
the layers under /overlayer, what each contains and who may change it;
how the layers are composed into the system view at boot;
where musl and glibc are installed and how programs linked against each find their loader, libraries, headers and compilers;
how software written for FHS systems is run;
the guarantees a package manager has to keep.

section.para: It does not specify the contents of configuration files, the init system, the desktop, or the package format.

section.title: Conventions
section.para: The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT and MAY are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

In paths, arch is the CPU architecture as it appears in a GNU target triplet (for example x86_64 or aarch64) and vendor is the vendor field of the triplet chosen by the implementation (for example zainium). A path written as /overlayer/syshub/bin names the directory in the composed system view unless the text says on disk.
Notes marked Implementation note describe how the reference implementation, Zainium OS, meets a requirement. They are informative, not normative.

section.title: Relationship to the FHS
section.para: DHS is not an extension of the FHS: a DHS system has no /usr, /bin, /lib or /etc at its root. Programs built for FHS systems still run, because their FHS paths are resolved to DHS paths when they are used (). lists where each FHS directory lives under DHS.
